source.title: Enhancing Corn Leaf Disease Classification Through Data Augmentation and Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: I. Fitriani; M. Mustakim; Matthew Qin; Laurice Tanap

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some table formatting is flattened, but the optimizer comparisons are described in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares optimizer performance on a natural image classification task using held-out evaluation, which bears on V4. It does not test the other mapped versions.
record.gate_note: The study does not use random labels, compare convolutional with fully connected networks, vary batch size, or ablate dropout. Architecture results are reported for two convolutional models only. Field testing is an out-of-distribution evaluation and is not used as evidence for the mapped versions. The 20-model table does not associate each row with a named optimizer, so those entries are not assigned to optimizer conditions.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares adaptive optimizers with SGD on held-out corn-leaf classification using pretrained ResNet50 and DenseNet169, extending V4 to a new transfer-learning setting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record correctly summarizes the optimizer averages but omits the authors' principal conclusion: ResNet50 with RMSprop, learning rate 0.001, augmentation, and the nominal 90:10 split achieved the best laboratory accuracy of 99.21%, while field accuracy fell to 70%. They conclude that training configuration and augmentation improve controlled-data performance but do not resolve field domain shift.
record.recipe_differences: A transfer-learning plant-disease classification experiment with fixed batch size and epoch count; it does not reproduce the original optimizer comparisons or their benchmark suite.
record.method_sensitivity: The optimizer comparison varies with data augmentation; the authors report separate optimizer performance under augmented and non-augmented conditions, but give numerical averages only for augmentation.

fits_no_version.finding: The selected model correctly classified 7 of 10 field images, versus 99.21% reported laboratory accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: High held-out accuracy on controlled plant images can coexist with substantially lower accuracy on field images.

record.peer_reviewed: Bulletin of Informatics and Data Science, Vol. 5 No. 1, May 2026
record.problems: Only two architectures and one task are studied. Numerical optimizer averages are given only for augmentation, and no uncertainty estimates or named per-optimizer results from the 20-model table can be recovered from its flattened layout. The reported field test is small and out-of-distribution, so it does not establish the mapped in-distribution claims.
record.rows_left_out: Table 5 lists metrics for 20 selected models but does not map rows to optimizer names in the supplied flattened text; these results were not assigned to optimizer conditions. Figure 8 values for non-augmentation conditions are not stated numerically.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label generalization using the same architecture and training recipe.
Width variation beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.

Language benchmarks, matched training performance, broader optimizer-specific tuning, learning-rate schedule comparisons, decoupled weight decay, and switching from Adam to SGD. The optimizer averages do not establish rankings after selecting each optimizer's best learning rate.
Batch-size comparisons; batch size is fixed at 32.
Dropout comparisons; dropout is included but never ablated or varied.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V4. Its local reversal does not refute the frequency qualifier 'often.' Optimizer averages have no uncertainty estimates or numerical SGD baseline, and their precise evaluation split and aggregation weights are unclear. Table 5's selected configurations lack optimizer mappings and cannot establish additional optimizer comparisons. Architecture and field-performance results do not test the other listed versions.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization on the same architecture and recipe.
Width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
Comparison with fully connected networks and local-connectivity effects.

The study evaluates optimizer accuracy in one corn-leaf classification task; it does not compare image-classification and language benchmarks, characterize tuning breadth, test switching from Adam to SGD, or use decoupled weight decay.
Large-batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout is included in the model heads but is not varied or ablated.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the train-test gap.
Removal of memorized examples and its effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: Nadam
rows.operation_detail: Compared average classification accuracy by optimizer across experiments.
rows.note: The authors state Nadam achieved the best performance with augmentation; they give no SGD value here.
rows.check: The reported 96.99% is correct. Nadam is an optimizer, not a model. Its comparison with SGD rests on the accompanying qualitative ranking; no numerical SGD baseline is supplied. This is an average across experimental configurations, not explicitly the best learning-rate-tuned performance.

rows.subject: Adamax
rows.operation_detail: Compared average classification accuracy by optimizer across experiments.
rows.note: The authors state Adamax remained superior on non-augmentation data, without giving a value there.
rows.check: The reported 96.21% is correct. Adamax is an optimizer, not a model. Its comparison with SGD rests on the accompanying qualitative ranking; no numerical SGD baseline is supplied. This is an average across experimental configurations, not explicitly the best learning-rate-tuned performance.

rows.subject: SGD
rows.operation_detail: Compared average classification accuracy by optimizer across experiments.
rows.value: Performed worst among the optimizers in this study.
rows.note: Qualitative outcome only; no numerical SGD accuracy is stated.
rows.check: The qualitative ranking is supported for both augmentation conditions. SGD is an optimizer, not a model. Its accuracy and the magnitude of its disadvantage are not stated.

relationships.condition: Average optimizer accuracy with augmentation in corn-leaf transfer learning, using five learning rates and 35 epochs
relationships.reason: R1–R3 report Nadam at approximately 96.99%, Adamax at 96.21%, and SGD ranked worst, reversing the adaptive-worse direction in this setting; these are configuration averages rather than best-tuned comparisons.
relationships.display_finding: Nadam and Adamax reportedly had the highest average accuracies while SGD ranked worst, but these configuration averages remain unverified.

relationships.condition: Average optimizer accuracy without augmentation in the same transfer-learning experiment
relationships.reason: R3's qualitative comparison states SGD performed worst; the accompanying text identifies Nadam and Adamax as remaining superior. No numerical disadvantage is supplied.
relationships.display_finding: SGD reportedly ranked below Nadam and Adamax without augmentation, but the qualitative comparison remains unverified.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: Nadam and Adamax are described as best with augmentation, while SGD performed worst; this reverses V4's expected adaptive-versus-SGD direction in this tested setting (R1–R3).
